title: Philadelphia Science Museum Closes as Supporters Seek to Reopen It
summary:
A familiar place for Philadelphia families has closed its doors. The Academy of Natural Sciences Museum announced on September 1 that it would close at the end of the month. Many families came for one last visit before the September 30 closure.

The Academy was founded in 1812 and opened to the public in 1828. In 1868, it became the first place in the world to display a dinosaur skeleton. Visitors could also explore animal displays and see live animals.

Drexel University has been responsible for the Academy's finances since 2011. It said costs had risen and fewer people had visited since the pandemic. During the final weeks, however, crowds grew sharply.

Supporters organized marches and a petition with more than 114,000 signatures. The William Penn Foundation offered a year of temporary funding. Drexel said it was exploring that offer, but would need a lasting financial plan before considering reopening.

The Academy holds more than 19 million scientific specimens. These are samples, such as fossils and plants, that researchers study. Drexel said students and researchers would keep access to the collection. Public access remains unclear.

Philadelphia's city council also plans public hearings to examine the closure and possible solutions. Whether or when the museum will reopen remains uncertain.
why_it_matters: The closure affects a place where generations of children explored natural history. Access to the collection for the public and the museum's possible reopening remain uncertain.
